deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is item 41 (attributed to N. Fuss), begun on p. 206. The problem is to solve λz² = μx² + νy² in integers, given one known solution λc² = μa² + νb².

On p. 206 Fuss multiplied and subtracted the two equations and factored the result: μ(cx+az)/(bz−cy) = ν(bz+cy)/(cx−az) = p/q. Solving each equality for z and equating the two values gave x = a(μνq²−p²) − 2νbpq and y = b(μνq²−p²) + 2μapq.

(1) Finishing the first solution: computing z. From the first equality, (z/c)(bp−μaq) = μqx + py. Substituting x and y:
- μqx + py = μ²ν a q³ − μν b pq² + μ a p²q − b p³
- this equals μaq(μνq²+p²) − bp(μνq²+p²)
- which equals (μνq²+p²)(μaq−bp).
Hence z/c = −(μνq²+p²), i.e. z = −c(μνq²+p²). The overall sign is immaterial because only z² enters.

(2) Alia solutio (second solution, by a multiplicative identity). Choose f, g, h with h² = f² + μνg². Multiply the known relation by it: λc²h² = μa²f² + μν²b²g² + νb²f² + μ²νa²g² = μ(af+νbg)² + ν(bf−μag)². The cross terms ±2μνabfg cancel; this is a Brahmagupta-type composition. So take z = ch, x = af+νbg, y = bf−μag. Use the standard parametrization of h² = f² + μνg²: f = μνq²−p², g = 2pq, h = μνq²+p². This gives
- x = a(μνq²−p²) + 2νbpq
- y = b(μνq²−p²) − 2μapq
- z = c(μνq²+p²).
This is the first solution with q → −q.

(3) Corollary: two variants obtained by moving a different term to the left.
- Variant II: write μx² = λz² − νy², μa² = λc² − νb². Apply the substitution (λ,μ,ν,z,x,y,c,a,b) → (μ,λ,−ν,x,z,y,a,c,b) with (p,q) → (r,s). This gives z = c(−λνs²−r²) − 2νbrs, y = b(−λνs²−r²) − 2λcrs, x = a(r²−λνs²).
- Variant III: write νy² = λz² − μx². Apply (λ,μ,ν,z,x,y,c,a,b) → (ν,λ,−μ,y,z,x,b,c,a) with (p,q) → (t,u). This gives z = c(−λμu²−t²) − 2μatu, x = a(−λμu²−t²) − 2λctu, y = b(t²−λμu²).

(4) Table of the three solutions, with overall signs normalized:
- I: x = a(μνq²−p²) + 2νbpq, y = b(μνq²−p²) − 2μapq, z = c(μνq²+p²).
- II: x = a(r²−λνs²), y = b(r²+λνs²) + 2λcrs, z = c(r²+λνs²) + 2νbrs.
- III: x = a(t²+λμu²) + 2λctu, y = b(t²−λμu²), z = c(t²+λμu²) + 2μatu.

The page remarks that the three columns yield the same numbers. Modern reading: all three are rational parametrizations of the same conic by the pencil of lines through the known point (a:b:c), so they agree up to proportionality.

(5) Example: 5z² = 2x² + 3y² with a = b = c = 1. The three forms become
- I: x = 6q²−p²+6pq, y = 6q²−p²−4pq, z = 6q²+p²
- II: x = r²−15s², y = r²+15s²+10rs, z = r²+15s²+6rs
- III: x = t²+10u²+10tu, y = t²−10u², z = t²+10u²+4tu.

Sample values:
- I, p = q = 1: (11,1,7).
- I, p = 1, q = −1: (±1,9,7).
- II, r = s = 1: (∓14,26,22) ∝ (7,13,11); check 605 = 98 + 507.
- II, r = 1, s = −1: (14,6,10) ∝ (7,3,5).
- III, t = u = 1: (21,±9,15) ∝ (7,3,5).
- III, t = 1, u = −1: (1,±9,7).

The repetition of (7,3,5) and (1,9,7) across the forms illustrates the remark.
errors: No mathematical errors found; every algebraic step and every numerical example checks.

Minor imprecisions only. The sign of z in the first solution (z = −c(...)) and of the corollary formulas is dropped silently in the table; this is harmless because the equation is homogeneous in squares.
The claim that the three formulas give 'the same numbers' holds only up to a common factor and sign. Examples: (21,9,15) vs (7,3,5); (14,26,22) vs (7,13,11).

results.what: Integer parametrization of all solutions of λz² = μx² + νy² from one known solution (a,b,c), by elimination/factoring (Fuss's first method).
results.modern_name: Rational parametrization of a conic via lines through a rational point (chord/secant method)
results.usually_credited_to: Diophantus (method); systematized by Fermat/Euler in the 18th century

results.what: Identity (μa²+νb²)(f²+μνg²) = μ(af+νbg)² + ν(bf−μag)², combined with f = μνq²−p², g = 2pq, h = μνq²+p², giving a second derivation.
results.modern_name: Brahmagupta-type composition identity for binary quadratic forms / norm multiplicativity
results.usually_credited_to: Brahmagupta (7th c.); Euler used such identities extensively

results.what: Three equivalent parametrizations obtained by permuting the roles of the variables (rearranging the equation), with the observation that they give the same solutions.
results.modern_name: Different coordinatizations of the pencil of lines through a point on a conic

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine 18th-century Diophantine analysis that is well documented in Euler's circle (his Algebra and his papers on quadratic forms). The fragment is attributed to N. Fuss and is a worked exercise on parametrizing a conic from a known point.

checkable.asserts: μqx + py = (μνq²+p²)(μaq − bp) for Fuss's x, y, so z = −c(μνq²+p²).
The composition identity used in the Alia Solutio.
f = μνq²−p², g = 2pq, h = μνq²+p² satisfies h² = f² + μνg².
Solution I satisfies λz² = μx² + νy² whenever λc² = μa² + νb².
Solution II satisfies the equation given the known solution.
Solution III satisfies the equation given the known solution.
